title: Bose Launches $99 USB-C Wired Earbuds With Active Noise Cancellation

author.name: Tech Desk
author.bio: The Tech Desk covers hardware releases, audio equipment, and broader consumer technology trends.

excerpt: Bose has returned to wired earbuds after 11 years with new $99 Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds featuring USB-C, ANC, lossless audio and no rechargeable battery.
seoTitle: Bose Launches $99 USB-C Wired Earbuds With ANC
seoDescription: Bose has returned to wired earbuds after 11 years with new $99 Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds featuring USB-C, ANC, lossless audio and no rechargeable battery.

content.text:
Bose is bringing wired listening back into its mainstream audio lineup with a new pair of noise-cancelling earbuds priced at $99. Announced on September 28, 2026, the Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds represent the company's first new wired earbuds in 11 years, combining an old-school wired design with technologies more commonly associated with premium Bluetooth headphones. Instead of relying on wireless connectivity and a rechargeable battery, the new earbuds plug directly into compatible devices through USB-C and draw their operating power from the connected phone, tablet or computer.

The launch comes as wired headphones are seeing renewed interest after years of declining popularity. WIRED, citing Circana data, reported that wired headphone sales increased 10% in the second half of 2025 and another 20% at the beginning of 2026. Bose executives have linked part of the resurgence to younger listeners, with wired earbuds becoming increasingly visible among Gen Z and Gen Alpha consumers. Bose president of consumer audio Raza Haider said the trend became particularly noticeable when visiting college campuses, influencing the company's decision to re-enter the category.

Bose's strategy is not simply to recreate an older pair of wired headphones. The new earbuds retain the straightforward plug-in experience while adding active noise cancellation, a feature historically associated with the company's wireless QuietComfort lineup. Bose says its proprietary QuietControl technology uses four microphones, with two located in each earbud, to monitor surrounding sound and reduce unwanted noise. Users can switch among Quiet Mode, Aware Mode and an ANC-Off mode using physical controls on the cable.

That design also eliminates one of the most familiar limitations of wireless earbuds: battery management. There is no internal rechargeable battery in the Bose wired model, and no Bluetooth pairing process is required. The earbuds instead receive power through the USB-C connection, allowing the noise-cancelling system and other electronics to operate directly from the connected device. Bose describes the setup as plug-and-play, with no companion app required.

The move to USB-C is equally significant. Bose has not revived the traditional 3.5mm headphone jack, instead building the product around the connector now found on many modern smartphones, tablets and laptops. The company says the earbuds use USB Audio Class 2 and proprietary digital signal processing to handle incoming audio, with playback output fixed at 24-bit/48kHz. Bose also highlights support for lossless listening and low-latency performance, making the earbuds suitable for video, gaming and content creation where synchronization can be important.

An inline remote is another key part of the design. Rather than placing touch controls on the earbuds, Bose uses physical buttons along the cable for volume, playback, calls and noise-cancellation modes. The central controller also contains a dedicated microphone intended to improve voice pickup while reducing unwanted noise caused by contact with clothing. Bose says users can operate the controls without needing to reach for a phone or press a button on the earbuds themselves.

The earbuds are designed to focus on everyday comfort as well as sound. Bose includes three sizes of silicone eartips and two sizes of stability wings, allowing users to create multiple combinations for fit. The company lists nine possible combinations of eartips and stability wings, while also noting that some listeners may prefer using the earbuds without the stabilizers. The cable measures 4.2 feet, giving users flexibility while carrying a phone or laptop during use.

Durability has also been addressed, although this is not positioned as a fully rugged sports product. The Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds carry an IPX4 rating, meaning they are designed to handle everyday exposure to sweat and splashes but are not intended for submersion or heavy water exposure. A zippered carrying case is included for storage. The earbuds launch in Black and White Smoke, alongside a limited-edition Dewdrop Mint version with a more retro-inspired appearance.

The $99 price places Bose's new product below the company's premium wireless noise-cancelling earbuds while still bringing active noise cancellation into a relatively inexpensive wired format. Bose currently lists the Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds at $99 in the United States, while its UK site lists the product at £99.95. The company has opened preorders in the United States through Bose and Best Buy, with shipping scheduled to begin October 15, 2026.

The product also reflects a broader shift in how consumers are thinking about audio hardware. Wireless earbuds have become the default for portability, but that convenience introduces batteries, charging cases, pairing processes and potential connectivity problems. Wired headphones remove several of those requirements. Bose is betting that some users will accept the physical cable in exchange for uninterrupted operation, predictable connectivity and very low latency. The result is a product that combines the simplicity of older headphones with the digital USB-C infrastructure of newer devices.

There are trade-offs. The wired design means users remain physically connected to their device, which can be less convenient than true wireless earbuds during movement. WIRED's early hands-on report also noted that the inline control module adds some weight and cable tension, and that the cable can become tangled when stored in the included pouch. Those observations came from an early unit rather than a full review, so long-term comfort and durability will require broader testing after retail availability.

Bose's return is notable because the wired-earbud market never completely disappeared even as wireless products dominated mainstream marketing. Affordable wired models have remained common, particularly for users seeking simplicity or avoiding battery-dependent accessories. Bose is entering that established market with a more recognizable premium feature set, particularly ANC, lossless-capable USB audio and a physical control system.

For Bose, the timing may be as important as the hardware itself. The company is launching the earbuds while wireless audio remains dominant but wired listening is gaining renewed visibility. The decision to develop the product in roughly eight to nine months, according to Haider, also reflects Bose's stated effort to accelerate product development and respond more quickly to changing consumer behavior.

The new earbuds could therefore become part of a wider revival of wired personal audio, particularly as USB-C becomes increasingly common across consumer electronics. Rather than treating wired listening as a purely nostalgic category, Bose is presenting it as a modern alternative built around battery-free operation, active noise cancellation and digital audio. At $99, the company is testing whether consumers interested in the return of wired headphones are willing to pay for a more sophisticated version of the familiar format.

For now, Bose's Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds are available for preorder at $99 in the U.S., with retail shipping scheduled for October 15. Their reception will likely depend on whether buyers value the combination of ANC, USB-C, low latency and battery-free operation enough to accept the inconvenience of a physical cable. The launch nevertheless marks a notable change in direction for one of the world's best-known headphone brands: after more than a decade away, Bose is once again making wired earbuds a central part of its consumer audio strategy.
